A Wall Street upgrade built on a shortage of server central processing unit (CPU) capacity has pushed Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) to the front of the chip group. Intel stock is at $91.36, up 5% in the session, a gain that puts it at the head of the semiconductor pack.

JasonDoiy / iStock Unreleased via Getty Images

Meanwhile, Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) stock is at $532.26, up 3%, following Intel shares higher at a slower clip. NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) shares are trading at $216.29, up 3%, keeping pace with AMD stock while staying behind Intel stock. This gap between the leader and its two big rivals suggests a stock-specific catalyst at work.

Chip-focused funds are running ahead of the wider technology complex. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX) is at $496.02, up 4%, a stronger showing than AMD or NVIDIA shares. By comparison, the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is at $714.41, up 1%, a far smaller lift for the large-cap technology benchmark.

Server CPU Shortage Drives New Street's Buy Call on Intel

New Street Research analyst Pierre Ferragu upgraded Intel to Buy from Neutral and set a $125 price target. Ferragu wrote, "Agentic AI is driving a sustained increase in server CPU demand, with supply constraints set to persist for years, while Intel is getting rid of bad nodes and adding capacity." title: Michael Burry Backs Ken Griffin’s “Obvious” GPU Warning as Market Risk Multiplies

Michael Burry Backs Ken Griffin's "Obvious" GPU Warning as Market Risk Multiplies ©pixelshot and Nikada from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Key Takeaways

Michael Burry said Ken Griffin's warning that GPU rental prices would go "into freefall" if supply ever passed demand is "obvious to most with a working brain cell."

The mechanism is real: in Nvidia's last downturn, in fiscal 2023, its gross margin fell to 56.9% from 64.9%.

A glut would cut into Nvidia's and AMD's sales, but CoreWeave would feel it first: its operating margin was -0.3% in 2025.

Rental prices still point to shortage, while consensus has Nvidia's revenue more than tripling over two fiscal years, to $692 billion.

Michael Burry doesn't think Ken Griffin's warning on GPU prices needs much debate.

On Monday, the investor best known for betting against housing before 2008 responded on X to a post summing up Griffin's bear case on AI chips. His answer took one line: "This is obvious to most with a working brain cell."

The timing is touchy. Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) fell about 4% in last Thursday's AI selloff, and the biggest cloud companies update their spending plans this week.

Griffin made his case last week on Bloomberg Talks. The Citadel CEO pointed back to the telecom buildout of 2000: "We built more fiber than we had demand for, and the price of telecommunications just went straight down."

He sees the same risk for AI chips: "if we reach a point where the provisioning of GPUs exceeds demand for GPUs, marginal pricing will actually go into freefall."

Once a GPU is installed, renting it out for another hour costs its owner very little. So in a glut, owners cut prices to keep their chips busy. Griffin said that "really upends all the investment assumptions that people are working with today." A glut would reach Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) through their customers' orders, and it would hit CoreWeave (CRWV:NASDAQ) directly, since GPU rentals are its revenue.

Burry has a point. Nvidia has already been through a version of this.

Nvidia's last downturn shows how fast pricing goes

Gross margin is the clearest measure of what scarcity is worth to Nvidia. The last time its sales stalled, in fiscal 2023 (the year ended January 2023), revenue was flat at $27.0 billion and gross margin fell to 56.9% from 64.9%.

It has stayed above 70% since then, and in the quarter ended July 2026 it was 75.0%.

Chicago, IL – October 26, 2026– Today, Zacks Investment Ideas feature highlights Bloom Energy BE, SanDisk SNDK, Advanced Micro Devices AMD, CoreWeave CRWV, Nebius Group NBIS, NVIDIA NVDA and SpaceX's SPCX.

The AI Rout: Sorting CapEx Fact from Fiction

Funding Fears Threaten AI Bull Market

Early in the year, investors rushed into tech stocks as AI innovations, investment, and rapid growth expectations drew attention away from the rest of the market. AI-related leaders like Bloom Energy, SanDisk and Advanced Micro Devices each soared more than 100%. However, over the past few months, Wall Street's price action has completely flipped. Although major market indices are within a hair of all-time highs, leading AI-stocks have been lackluster, with many down 50% or more off their 2026 highs.

What Caused the Destruction in AI Stocks?
Gravity & Profit Taking

First, while the correction in AI-related names is undoubtedly painful for bulls (especially those who bought near the highs), corrections of this magnitude are normal in bull markets. For example, SanDisk exploded by ~2,800% from August 2025 to June 2026. In other words, after such a massive move, profit taking is to be expected. Currently, SanDisk is testing its rising 200-day moving average, the best gauge of the long-term trend, for the first time in its history. Again, even the strongest stocks occasionally succumb to the laws of gravity.

The AI Debt Fear Narrative

More recently, selling in AI stocks has intensified amid a sharp shift in Wall Street sentiment regarding AI spending and the sustainability of debt loads. The tipping point came when neocloud leader CoreWeave saw its unsecured bonds dumped, pushing yields to a distressed 15%. In other words, the move in CoreWeave's bonds suggests fixed-income investors have far less confidence in the company's ability to meet its ballooning debt. So far in October, CoreWeave shares have plunged nearly 40%, dragging other neocloud and AI -related stocks like Nebius Group along with it.

CoreWeave, which started as a Bitcoin Mining company, pivoted to AI data centers during the 2022 crypto bear market. Today, it is a specialized AI cloud provider that rents out massive clusters of graphics processing units (GPUs) and infrastructure to companies training and running AI models. Building massive AI data centers requires heavy upfront expenses for CoreWeave because its business model demands immediate, large-scale capital spending on infrastructure and hardware before it collects cash from customer contracts.
